Part 4 of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: 3 · Throughput calculatorNext: 5 · Empirical rooflines

We now present a set of exercises to get a better grasp and intuition on those rooflines. Here, the idea is to perform some napkin math so the answers to those exercises is more about getting the formula and the leading order (or trend) right than it is about precise numerics.

Exercise 1: reading the roofline

Figure 15 · interactive

Roofline graph.

In Questions 1 and 2, we focus on the case of short context, i.e., a 1k context. Hence, the network can be approximated by its linear layers.

  1. Heights and throughput. What is the relationship between the heights of the two points and the throughput gain \(\Gamma\)?

    Solution

    First, let us describe what the roofline graph is plotting. On the roofline graph, the \(y\)-axis is describing how much FLOPs are consumed per second. We recall that one forward pass corresponds to \(F\) FLOPs. The time for one forward pass is the maximum between the time it takes to perform calculations and the time it takes to move bytes. Hence, we have

    \[ T = \max\left( \frac{F}{\pi}, \frac{Q}{\beta}\right), \]

    Hence, the attainable FLOP/s \(R\), i.e., the height of a point on the roofline graph, is given by

    \[ R = F/T = \pi \min\left( 1, \frac{F \beta}{Q \pi}\right) = \pi \min\left( 1, \frac{I}{I^\star}\right). \]

    Hence, on a logarithmic scale we have

    \[ \log_{10}(R) = \log_{10}(\pi) + \min\left( 0, \log_{10}(I) - \log_{10}(I^\star) \right). \]

    Denote \(\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}} = \pi \min \left( 1, \frac{\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{I^{\star}}\right)\) and \(\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \pi \min \left( 1, \frac{\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{I^{\star}}\right)\). Then the ratio of the heights is given by

    \[ \frac{\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}}} = \frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}, I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)} . \]

    Now, we recall from Proposition 1 that, with \(\omega = Sr + 1\), \(S\) the number of denoising passes and \(r\) the cost of a denoising pass relative to a commit pass, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}},I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}},I^\star)}. \]

    Therefore, we get

    \[ \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\class{mj-td}{R^{\mathrm{TD}}}}{\class{mj-ar}{R^{\mathrm{AR}}}}. \]

    This means that the throughput gain is proportional to the ratio of the heights on the roofline, with constant \(1/\omega\).

  2. The best batch. Find where on the graph \(\Gamma\) is largest, and estimate \(\Gamma\) there.

    Solution

    AR is memory-bound here, since its intensity is about 2, far below \(I^\star = 206\). Hence, according to Corollary 1, we have that

    \[ \Gamma = \min\left(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}, \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\right) . \]

    Now, we have \(\frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi} \leq \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\) if and only if \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \leq I^\star\), since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} = \frac{b \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}{\Pi}\). Hence, while TD is on the slope of the roofline graph, we have \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\).

    Since the network can be approximated by its linear layers, we have that \(\Pi \approx \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = \frac{\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B)}{\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)}\), where we recall that \(W^X\) is the number of weights, in parameters, that the method \(X\) reads. In particular, with a canvas size \(256\), we have that \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B) \approx W_{\mathrm{tot}}\), even at \(B=1\), since all the experts are touched. Since \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) increases with \(B\), \(\Pi\) is non-increasing in \(B\), and Corollary 1 (2) applies: \(\Gamma\) is largest at the batch \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star}\) at which TD reaches the ridge.

    Indeed, while TD is memory-bound, \(\Gamma = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}\) increases with \(B\). Once TD becomes compute-bound, i.e., \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \geq I^\star\), it stays compute-bound, since \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}\) is non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1). Since \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) is also non-decreasing in \(B\) (Lemma 1), \(\Gamma = \frac{I^\star}{\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}}\) then decreases. Hence, the optimal point is reached when TD just becomes compute-bound, i.e., just at the beginning of the flat roofline for TD.

    On the graph this happens for \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \approx 6\), and the height ratio is then \(\approx 100\). Remembering the previous formula, we have then \(\Gamma \approx 100 / 15 \approx 6.5\), where we recall that \(\omega=15\).

  3. Large context. What changes at large context?

    Solution

    At large context, the KV cache carries most of the bytes and most of the FLOPs of both passes, and Corollary 3 applies. A cache belongs to one sequence, so its bytes and FLOPs per sequence do not depend on the batch: the two points, and \(\Gamma\), no longer move with the batch. On a global layer, a TD pass reads the same cache as an AR step and performs \(b\) times its FLOPs, so \(\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}} = 1\), \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\) and \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 2{,}048\). AR stays on the slope and TD on the roof, so the height ratio tends to \(I^\star/I_{\mathrm{attn}} \approx 206/8 \approx 26\) and

    \[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega\, I_{\mathrm{attn}}} \approx \frac{26}{15} \approx 1.7 . \]

    TD still wins, but by much less than the 6.5 of Question 2: AR's point moves right, from an intensity of about 2 to 8, while TD's point cannot rise above the roof. At batch 6, the cache, at 20 kB per token, reaches AR's 3 GB of weights per sequence near 150k tokens.

Exercise 2: the gain along the batch

Figure 16

  1. Batch 1. Shrinking the canvas from 256 to 32 divides TPF by 8. Predict whether it also divides the penalty \(\Pi\) by 8, then give \(\Gamma\) at batch 1.

    Hint 1

    With the halving rule, what fraction of the experts does a 32-token canvas leave untouched?

    Solution

    \(\mathrm{TPF} = 32/15 \approx 2.1\). A canvas of 32 tokens leaves \((15/16)^{32} \approx 2^{-3} = 1/8\) of the experts untouched, so \(\Pi_E \approx 16 \times 7/8 = 14\). The \(k\) active experts are \(LkW^e \approx 30 \times 8 \times 6\text{M} \approx 1.4\)B of AR's 3.1B parameters, so \(\theta_E \approx 1/2\) and \(\Pi \approx 1 + \tfrac12 \times 13 = 7.5\). TD's intensity is \(32/7.5 \approx 4\) times AR's, both points are on the slope, and \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi \approx 0.3\): AR wins. The penalty falls only from 8 to 7.5 while TPF falls 8 times, because the attention and dense weights, half of AR's bytes, are read once per pass whatever \(b\). On the map, the bottom of the column is blue.

  2. TD starts winning. From which batch does TD win?

    Hint 1

    Both decoders are still memory-bound, so \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi(B)\). Which of \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}}(B)\) and \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) still grows with the batch?

    Hint 2

    How many experts must AR touch per layer for \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) to reach \(W_{\mathrm{tot}}/\mathrm{TPF}\)?

    Solution

    From batch 2 on, a TD pass covers at least 64 tokens, which leave \(2^{-6}\) of the experts untouched, so \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx W_{\mathrm{tot}} = 24.5\)B and only \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) still grows. \(\Gamma = 1\) needs \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B) = 24.5/2.1 \approx 11.5\)B, that is, \(30 \times U_{E,k}(B) \times 6\text{M} \approx 10\)B and \(U_{E,k}(B) \approx 55\). The untouched fraction is then \(1 - 55/128 \approx 0.57 \approx 2^{-0.8}\), so \(1.5B/16 \approx 0.8\) and \(B \approx 9\). TD's intensity there is about \(bBN_{\mathrm{act}}/W_{\mathrm{tot}} \approx 32 \times 9 \times 3.1/24.5 \approx 36\), still on the slope, as Hint 1 assumed. TD starts winning because the penalty is a ratio, and AR's own coverage of the experts grows with the batch. On the map, this is the lower branch of the thick dashed line \(\Gamma = 1\).

  3. The best batch. TPF is 8 times smaller than at \(b = 256\). Predict whether the best gain is 8 times smaller than the \(\Gamma \approx 6.5\) of Exercise 1, then find the best batch and its gain.

    Hint 1

    Where on the roofline did the gain peak in Exercise 1, Question 2?

    Hint 2

    With \(\class{mj-td}{W^{\mathrm{TD}}} = W_{\mathrm{tot}}\), \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx bBN_{\mathrm{act}}/W_{\mathrm{tot}}\). How does the corner batch scale with \(b\), and how many experts does AR leave untouched there?

    Solution

    The gain peaks when TD's point reaches the corner: \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}} \approx 32B/8 = 4B\) reaches 206 at \(B \approx 51\), eight times the best batch at \(b = 256\), since \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \propto 1/b\) (Corollary 2). With the 1k cache of Question 4, a TD pass spends \(32 \times 6.8 \approx 216\) GFLOPs per sequence on \(49/B + 0.22\) GB, which moves the corner to about 60. At batch 51, AR leaves \(2^{-1.5 \times 51/16} \approx 2^{-5} \approx 3\%\) of the experts untouched, so \(\Pi \approx 1\) and \(\Gamma \approx \mathrm{TPF} \approx 2.1\). The best gain is about 3 times smaller, not 8: at \(b = 256\) the best batch, 6, still pays \(\Pi \approx 24.5/9 \approx 2.7\), whereas a short canvas reaches the corner only at a batch where AR touches nearly every expert. On the map, the darkest orange lies below the solid line labelled "TD compute-bound above", and the peak is lower, about 1.8, because of the vocabulary matrix.

  4. TD loses again. At which batch does AR catch up? Predict whether this batch depends on \(b\).

    Hint 1

    Above the corner, \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}})\) (Corollary 1). Does \(b\) appear in it?

    Hint 2

    Per sequence, an AR step reads \(49/B\) GB of weights. Which bytes does it also read that do not shrink with \(B\), and at what intensity?

    Solution

    \(\Gamma = 1\) when \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} = 206/15 \approx 14\), and \(b\) does not appear: parity is at the same batch for every canvas long enough to reach the roof. Without a cache, \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx B/8\) and parity would be at batch 110 (Corollary 2). At 1k tokens, a sequence also reads 0.2 GB of window cache at intensity 2 and 0.02 GB of global cache at intensity 8, so its step costs \(6.2 + 0.4 + 0.16 \approx 6.8\) GFLOPs for \(49/B + 0.22\) GB. Setting the ratio to 14 gives \(49/B \approx 0.27\), so parity is at about batch 180: the window cache, whose intensity is below AR's at these batches, lowers AR's average intensity (Proposition 2). On the map, the upper branch of the thick dashed line sits near batch 110 rather than 180, because of the vocabulary matrix; its agreement with the no-cache estimate is a coincidence.

Exercise 3: a dense model

We take a dense model, Llama 3.1 8B, on the H200, and pair it with a TD twin that has no self-conditioning. A dense model has no expert penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = 1\), and in BF16 its linear intensity is the batch: \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(B) = 2BN_{\mathrm{act}}/(2N_{\mathrm{act}}) = B\).

Figure 17

For a dense model, the roofline bound at context 1k is about 13 at batch 1 and falls like 1/B, to parity at batch 15.

  1. No penalty. With \(\Pi = 1\), a colleague expects \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF} \approx 17\) at batch 1 and short context. Find the flaw, give \(\Gamma\), and give the parity batch.

    Hint 1

    Where is TD's point at batch 1? Compare \(b\,I_{\mathrm{lin}}(1)\) with \(I^\star\).

    Hint 2

    With TD at the roof, at which \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) is \(\Gamma = 1\)?

    Solution

    \(b\,I_{\mathrm{lin}}(1) = 256 \gt 206\): TD's point is at the roof already at batch 1, and TPF/\(\Pi\) is not the smaller term of Corollary 1. Hence \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}) = 206/15 \approx 14\), the largest batch-1 gain of these exercises, and \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega B) = 1\) at batch 14. Compared with Exercise 2, the first three events coincide at batch 1: without a penalty there is no losing phase, and the best batch is batch 1. On the map, the bottom row is dark orange, and the thick dashed line \(\Gamma = 1\) lies near batch 14.

  2. The cache and the ridge. At a 1k context, can any batch make AR compute-bound?

    Hint 1

    In Exercise 2, Question 4, which bytes per sequence did not shrink with the batch? What happens to the others as \(B \to \infty\)?

    Hint 2

    A sequence's cache holds 131 kB per token and is read at intensity 4. Compute AR's intensity once the weights have vanished.

    Solution

    The weights are shared by the batch, so their bytes per sequence vanish as \(B \to \infty\); the cache belongs to one sequence and stays. At 1k tokens a sequence reads \(1\text{k} \times 131\,\text{kB} \approx 0.13\) GB of cache, which carries \(4 \times 0.13 \approx 0.5\) GFLOPs, next to the \(2N_{\mathrm{act}} = 14\) GFLOPs of the linear layers. AR's intensity therefore tends to \(14.5/0.13 \approx 110 \lt 206\), and no batch makes AR compute-bound (Proposition 9). Hence the gain keeps falling with the batch towards \(206/(15 \times 110) \approx 0.12\), above the \(1/\omega \approx 0.07\) that a compute-bound AR would give: at batch 256, a sequence reads \(14/256 \approx 0.055\) GB of weights and 0.13 GB of cache for 14.5 GFLOPs, so \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 78\) and \(\Gamma \approx 206/(15 \times 78) \approx 0.18\). AR can reach the ridge only if \(14\,\text{GFLOPs}/Q_c + 4 \gt 206\) for a cache of \(Q_c\) bytes, that is, \(Q_c \lt 70\) MB, or about 530 tokens. On the map, the 1k column stays blue above batch 15.

Exercise 4: a low ridge and the vocabulary

We go back to DiffusionGemma, on an H20, whose ridge point is about a fifth of the H200's (Table 3).

Figure 18

On an H20, whose ridge point is 37, the roofline bound puts TD ahead of AR only up to batch 4 at short context.

  1. What Proposition 1 leaves out. Proposition 1 ignores the vocabulary matrix, which DiffusionGemma's TD applies as the head of every denoising pass and, for self-conditioning, as a soft embedding in all but the first (Part 1, What the formulas leave out). At which batches does this omission overstate \(\Gamma\), on the H20 and on the H200, and by how much? What does it do to parity on the H20?

    Hint 1

    The matrix adds FLOPs and bytes to both decoders. Which decoder is compute-bound, and from which batch, on each accelerator? Does a compute-bound pass slow down with extra FLOPs or with extra bytes?

    Hint 2

    How many vocabulary-sized multiplications does a TD position meet per committed token, and how large is \(2Vd\) next to \(2N_{\mathrm{act}}\)?

    Solution

    Applying the matrix to one position costs \(2Vd \approx 1.5\) GFLOPs, 24% of \(2N_{\mathrm{act}} \approx 6.2\) GFLOPs. A TD position goes through \(\omega = 15\) passes but meets the matrix \(2S - 1 = 27\) times: as the head of the 14 denoising passes, and as the soft embedding of self-conditioning in 13 of them. Once TD is compute-bound, its FLOPs, and hence its time, grow by a factor \(1 + 27 \times 0.24/15 \approx 1.43\). AR is memory-bound, and at a few sequences the matrix adds 0.74B parameters to the 8B its step reads, a factor 1.1. Where TD is compute-bound, the omission therefore overstates \(\Gamma\) by 1.43 divided by AR's own slowdown, \(1 + 0.74/\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}(B)\) with \(\class{mj-ar}{W^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) in billions: about 1.3 at a few sequences, and 1.4 once AR reads all 24.5B parameters. This holds on the H20 from a few sequences on, because TD's batch-1 intensity, about 32, is already near the ridge and the matrix's FLOPs push it over; on the H200 only above \(\class{mj-td}{B^{\mathrm{TD}}_\star} \approx 6\), which moves the parity of Exercise 2 from about 180 to about 110. Below that batch, the matrix's bytes raise \(\Gamma\) slightly, since they weigh more in AR's bytes than in TD's.

    On the H20, parity without the matrix is at \(I_{\mathrm{lin}}(B) = 37/15 \approx 2.5\). At batch 10, \(2^{-0.9} \approx 1/2\) of the experts are untouched, so AR touches 64 per layer, reads \(1.7 + 30 \times 64 \times 6\text{M} \approx 13\)B parameters, and \(I_{\mathrm{lin}} \approx 10 \times 3.1/13 \approx 2.4\): parity is near batch 10. With the matrix, parity needs \(I_{\mathrm{lin}} \approx 2.5/1.3 \approx 1.9\). At batch 5, \(2^{-0.5} \approx 0.7\) of the experts are untouched, AR touches 38 per layer, reads \(1.7 + 30 \times 38 \times 6\text{M} \approx 8.5\)B parameters, and \(I_{\mathrm{lin}} \approx 15.5/8.5 \approx 1.8\): parity moves to about batch 5. A low ridge puts TD's whole winning range in the compute-bound regime, where every FLOP that Proposition 1 omits costs gain. On the map, which counts the matrix, the thick dashed line \(\Gamma = 1\) crosses the 1k column near batch 5.

Exercise 5: sparse attention

We go back to the H200 and replace DiffusionGemma's five global layers with the sparse layers of Remark 1 (Table 3), as in Figure 11.

  1. The limit. As the context grows, does TD win with \(S = 14\)? Up to which \(S\) does it win? Predict, then check the case \(S = 14\) against the shading of Figure 11, which is drawn for \(S = 14\).

    Hint 1

    As \(C \to \infty\), the scan carries most of the bytes and FLOPs of both passes. Where are \(I_{\mathrm{idx}}\) and \(b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}}\) relative to \(I^\star\) (Corollary 3)?

    Hint 2

    Which of \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\), \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}\), \(\Pi\) and \(\omega\) changes when \(S\) changes?

    Solution

    \(I_{\mathrm{idx}} = 16 \lt 206 \lt b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}} = 4{,}096\): TD's scan is compute-bound and AR's memory-bound, so \(\Gamma \to 206/(15 \times 16) \approx 0.86\), and AR wins. AR runs its scan at \(16/206 \approx 8\%\) of the peak, and per committed token TD's 15 passes at the peak take longer than AR's step, since \(15 \gt 206/16 \approx 13\). Only \(\omega = Sr + 1\) depends on \(S\), so \(\Gamma \propto 1/\omega\) at every batch and context, and \(206/(16\omega) \gt 1\) needs \(\omega \lt 13\): \(S \le 11\). Dense attention, at \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\), allows \(S \le 24\). The limit assumes \(b\,I_{\mathrm{idx}} \gt I^\star\), a canvas of at least 13 positions; on a shorter canvas both scans are memory-bound and \(\Gamma \to \mathrm{TPF}\), below 1. In Figure 11, the shaded region \(\Gamma \lt 1\) reaches the right edge.

  2. Far from the limit. At 4M tokens, Figure 11 is shaded: Corollary 3 gives \(\Gamma \lt 1\). Does AR win at batch 1 with \(S = 14\)? Find the assumption that fails.

    Hint 1

    List what an AR step reads at batch 1 and 4M tokens: weights, window cache, index cache. Which carries most of the bytes, and what does Corollary 3 assume?

    Hint 2

    TD's 256 queries select \(U_{C,m}(b)\) distinct tokens, read from the global cache at 20 kB each. Compute \(\Pi\) and both terms of Corollary 1.

    Solution

    The index cache holds 640 B per token, so 4M tokens take 2.7 GB, against 6.2 GB of weights and 0.2 GB of window cache: the assumption of Corollary 3 fails, since the weights still carry most of AR's bytes. The index cache is about 0.3 of AR's bytes and the weights 0.7, so \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 0.7 \times 1 + 0.3 \times 16 \approx 5.5\). TD's 256 queries select \(U_{C,m}(b) \approx bm \approx 520\)k distinct tokens, since \(bm \ll C\), about 10.5 GB of global cache. TD reads about \(49 + 2.7 + 10.5 \approx 62\) GB against AR's 9 GB, so \(\Pi \approx 7\) and \(\mathrm{TPF}/\Pi \approx 17/7 \approx 2.4\), while \(I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}) \approx 206/(15 \times 5.5) \approx 2.5\). TD sits at the ridge and \(\Gamma \approx 2.4\): TD wins. Parity at batch 1 needs \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 14\), hence an index cache near 87% of AR's bytes, about 40 GB or 60M tokens. At 4M tokens the global cache alone is about 85 GB, and the 141 GB of an H200 hold the weights and at most about 4.3M tokens of cache, so on one H200 the limit of Question 1 is out of reach.

Exercise 6: number formats

We keep DiffusionGemma on the H200 at a 1k context, and change the format of the weights, of the KV cache and of the matrix multiplications. A format of \(s\) bytes per value multiplies the intensity of what it stores by \(2/s\): \(s_w\) acts on \(I_{\mathrm{lin}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{kv}}\) on \(I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 4g/(\kappa^c_\ell s_{\mathrm{kv}})\) (Definitions 1–3). The format of a multiplication sets the peak, and hence the ridge, at which its FLOPs run. The questions follow the roofline chapter of How to Scale Your Model, which compares int8 weights with BF16 and with int8 multiplications.

  1. A common speed-up. Weights and cache are in FP8, and every multiplication, attention included, runs at the FP8 peak. A colleague argues that this favours TD, which is compute-bound at its best batch and gains from the doubled peak. Find the flaw: does \(\Gamma\) change?

    Hint 1

    What does FP8 do to the time of a memory-bound AR step? Then: what happens to \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\), \(\class{mj-td}{I^{\mathrm{TD}}}\) and \(I^\star\) in Proposition 1?

    Solution

    A memory-bound AR step reads half the bytes, so it also runs twice as fast. Every intensity doubles and the ridge doubles, so both minima of Proposition 1 double and \(\Gamma\) does not change at any batch or context. A format changes \(\Gamma\) only when it speeds up the bytes and the FLOPs by different factors. An FP8 cache read by BF16 attention is such a case: \(I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) doubles to 16 while the ridge of attention stays at 206, and the long-context limit falls to \(206/(15 \times 16) \approx 0.86\), as with the index scan of Exercise 5.

  2. Fewer bytes than FLOPs. NVFP4 weights, once on the H200, which has no FP4 multiplication and converts them to BF16, and once on the B200, which multiplies them at its FP4 peak; the cache stays in BF16. Predict which setting acts like a lower BF16 ridge, then give each one's best gain.

    Hint 1

    The weight intensities grow by \(2/s_w\), and the ridge by the speed-up of the multiplications. Divide all intensities and the ridge by \(2/s_w\): which BF16 roofline remains?

    Hint 2

    On that BF16 roofline, redo Exercise 1, Question 2: where does \(32B\) reach the ridge, and what is \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}}\) there?

    Solution

    Let \(\rho\) be the speed-up of the multiplications divided by \(2/s_w\). \(\Gamma\) depends only on the intensities divided by the ridge (Question 1), so each setting acts like BF16 on an accelerator with ridge \(\rho I^\star\). The solution neglects the BF16 cache, which at 1k tokens is a sixth to a quarter of AR's bytes at these batches once the weights are in NVFP4, and raises the gains below by about 15%. With \(s_w \approx 0.56\) (Table 3), \(2/s_w \approx 3.6\).

    • H200: \(\rho = 1/3.6\), so the ridge is \(206/3.6 \approx 57\). The corner is near batch 2, where AR touches 15 experts per layer and reads \(1.7 + 30 \times 15 \times 6\text{M} \approx 4.4\)B parameters, so \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 2 \times 3.1/4.4 \approx 1.4\) and \(\Gamma \approx 57/(15 \times 1.4) \approx 2.7\).
    • B200: \(\rho = 4/3.6 \approx 1.1\), so the ridge is \(1{,}125/3.6 \approx 310\). The corner is at \(B \approx 10\), where AR leaves \(2^{-0.94} \approx 0.52\) of the experts untouched, touches 61 per layer and reads \(1.7 + 30 \times 61 \times 6\text{M} \approx 12.7\)B parameters, so \(\class{mj-ar}{I^{\mathrm{AR}}} \approx 10 \times 3.1/12.7 \approx 2.4\) and \(\Gamma \approx 310/(15 \times 2.4) \approx 9\), against about 8 at the B200's BF16 ridge of 281.

    When the weight bytes shrink by more than the multiplications speed up, \(\rho \lt 1\) and the setting acts like a lower ridge, which lowers both the best batch and the best gain (Corollary 2). FP8 weights converted to BF16, as on an A100, which has no FP8 rate, give \(\rho = 1/2\): the batch at which a multiplication becomes compute-bound halves, as in How to Scale Your Model. NVFP4 on the B200 has \(\rho \gt 1\) and acts like a higher ridge. At batch 1, every setting keeps both decoders on the slope, and \(\Gamma \approx 2.1\).
